files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller's checklist

Owner: D. Lindqvist. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts.

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, prepare one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July; some months, every run pays in-month. If such a period exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule, supporting contracts, and the GL. If it is missing, record ONE combined journal entry—do not duplicate an entry already posted. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month a prepaid item begins.
4. Record June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after verifying the GL to avoid a duplicate posting.
5. Check every June vendor bill against its source document and verify the expense coding. Reclass anything miscoded.
6. Draft June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after items 1-5 have been posted.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Stonebridge Professional Services began in 2018 when two former operations consultants decided that smaller organizations deserved the same disciplined project support typically reserved for large enterprises. They built the firm around a straightforward promise: experienced people, practical recommendations, and work products clients can actually use.

The company provides project management, process improvement, operational planning, reporting support, and short-term advisory services. Engagements range from focused diagnostic work to hands-on implementation, with teams assembled according to the client’s needs rather than a rigid service package. Much of the work comes from repeat clients and referrals from legal, accounting, technology, and marketing partners.

Stonebridge has a compact, collaborative team. Senior consultants remain close to delivery, while coordinators keep schedules, documentation, and client follow-ups moving. The culture is polished but unpretentious: meetings start on time, drafts are expected to be useful, and nobody is too senior to fix a messy tracker. A small network of specialist contractors adds depth when an engagement calls for niche expertise.

The firm is currently refining its market positioning, strengthening partner relationships, and standardizing internal close and project-review routines. Day to day, the emphasis remains on serving existing clients well while building a steadier pipeline of well-matched advisory work.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## Direction
Position Stonebridge Professional Services as the practical partner for organizations that need experienced project leadership without unnecessary ceremony. The voice should be confident, useful, and human.

## Priorities

- Refresh the brand story and core service pages so prospects can quickly understand what Stonebridge does, how engagements work, and when to call.
- Publish client-friendly insights drawn from recurring operational problems, with an emphasis on checklists, field notes, and short case examples.
- Host two webinars per quarter. Keep the format conversational and leave room for live questions.
- Test a partner co-marketing pilot with complementary legal, accounting, technology, or creative firms.
- Build a simple follow-up rhythm for former clients, referral partners, and qualified prospects.

## Quarter focus

### Q3
Complete messaging work, update priority web pages, assemble the first webinar topics, and recruit pilot partners. Create reusable promotion and follow-up templates.

### Q4
Run the partner pilot, continue the webinar series, and turn the strongest sessions into articles and short-form posts. Gather client language that can sharpen future case studies.

## Measures
Track qualified conversations, referral activity, webinar attendance, follow-up engagement, and opportunities influenced by content. Review results at each quarter-end and keep only the activities that produce credible interest.
files.notes/prior_accountant_memo.md:
# Notes from your predecessor

D. Lindqvist — a few things worth knowing before you settle into the close:

- The bank tends to slip its own fees and service charges onto the last few lines of the statement. That is normal here; we have historically booked those at close rather than during the month.
- June got busy, and some vendor-bill expense coding may be off. Check the underlying paperwork and treat the documents in `bills/` as the authoritative source. If the GL disagrees, the bill wins.
- The budget was locked early in the quarter. The one-off June items were not contemplated when it was set, so they should account for most of the larger budget-to-actual variances.
- One payroll caution: do not guess based on the usual cadence. The pay date for the second monthly run varies. Check the payroll register and follow the date shown there.
